headlines.title: AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.
headlines.summary: Credit markets will be closely watching updates from Oracle and other hyperscalers later this week. What to expect.
headlines.article_text: AI debt outlook: Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon in focus Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Meta's negative free cash flow sent its credit default spreads and bond yields higher, but its announced equity offering on Monday helped calm nerves. Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results this week. Investors will be watching capex spending plans and potential for debt issuance. In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A drone view shows a data center at the Google Storey County Campus in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center in Sparks, Nevada, US Oct. 9, 2026. Daniel Cole | Reuters Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming. Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively. Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms ' plans for a $95 billion stock offering , announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off. Meta's five-year credit default swaps on Oct. 27, 2026 Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief. "Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said. A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer. Fears 'overblown' The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. "I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks." Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%. Amazon's five-year credit default swaps on Oct. 27, 2026 Bond yields also remain elevated. "It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment." Earnings in focus Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft 's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending. Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to have continue. Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion. S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027. More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space." Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said. CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-1, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P. "It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one." Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Oct. 27, 2026. Off-balance sheet debt One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report. "There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Monday. S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added. watch now VIDEO 4:09 04:09 S&P Global's Mark Habib on why hyperscalers likely have more AI debt than investors realize Squawk on the Street Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose. Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis. "They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers. "The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. headlines.article_text: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps, expands cloud chip lineup Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Oracle is adding OpenAI's ChatGPT and Codex to its application stack, extending enterprise access to OpenAI tools. Oracle said OCI will add Google TPUs, OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras hardware as customers seek more silicon options. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk for a keynote at Oracle AI World. In this article OPENAI.FG CBRS ORCL GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable. Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT "allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET. For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab's push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor, Anthropic , filed its S-1 as it heads toward an initial public offering . Oracle's database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct. 27, 2026. CNBC Thiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits. "More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release. Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, including Google 's tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip. "Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI," Thiagarajan said. It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs. Thiagarajan added that the scarcity of chips remains an ongoing issue and that customers such as OpenAI can benefit from having different accelerators to choose from. When asked whether this marks a pivot away from Nvidia GPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are "the best, most fungible," and that the AI market remains incredibly large. OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras will also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won't be disclosing the scale because it's in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said. Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday. Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle's multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it's receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company. "We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure," he said. A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backer Blue Owl Capital last month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule. Investors are now counting down to Oracle's investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital. Bank of America analysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle's major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting. headlines.title: CNBC Workforce Executive Summit live updates: How AI is reshaping work and jobs
headlines.summary: Follow CNBC's 2026 Workforce Executive Summit for live updates on Walmart's AI strategy, changing job skills, hiring, employee benefits and the future of work.
headlines.article_text: CNBC Workforce Executive Summit 2026 live updates: AI at work Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu CNBC Workforce Executive Council members speak with CNBC's Sharon Epperson at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 27, 2026. CNBC Today's workplace faces a litany of challenges. Whether it's shifting power dynamics between employers and employees, the accelerating impact of artificial intelligence on how we work and the skills we need, or the financial stresses that employees of all ranks are feeling, these issues and more are challenging the cohesion of workplace communities. To address these issues, CNBC is convening its premiere council of human resource executives in New York City on Tuesday for the annual CNBC Workforce Executive Summit. The event is exclusive to members of CNBC's Workforce Executive Council. For more about the WEC and to apply for membership, visit www.cnbccouncils.com/wec . 41 Min Ago The benefit workers want the most? "Paid on time," says DailyPay's Chai DailyPay CEO Nelson Chai speaks with CNBC's Sharon Epperson at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 27, 2026. CNBC The majority of Americans are living paycheck-to-paycheck. DailyPay CEO Nelson Chai told CNBC's Sharon Epperson that in light of this, their top priorities are not benefits like "the gym membership or pet insurance or some of those things that are things they can add on to." "They mostly want to get paid on time. They need to figure out how to get to work. They need to figure out how to put food on the table," he said. "So those are the things we're really focused in on." The way companies provide health insurance, too, Chai said, is already beginning to evolve. "Healthcare is continuing to migrate to a menu where [companies] give them healthcare dollars and you pick out how you're going to allocate your dollars," he said. Over time, he said, "it'll be more efficient for employers to not offer things that don't really add value, and it'll be way more impactful for the folks who need access to their paychecks." -Colleen McKown 1 Hour Ago Steve Cadigan: Mistake companies are making is "using the old tech playbook" watch now VIDEO 4:51 04:51 Steve Cadigan: The real value of AI is in finding ways to create more As AI integrates itself into workplaces, Steve Cadigan, Human Advantage Framework creator and author, told CNBC's Leslie Picker that companies are struggling to realize the promise of the technology. "I think the mistake a lot of us are making is we're using the old tech playbook, which is to use technology to go faster, do more, and save money," he said. "Do I think AI can deliver, go faster, do more, save money? 100% it can. But I think where the real value is is in finding ways to create more." Cadigan pointed out that leadership is more burnt out than ever. "It's an all-time low. I mean, it's blinking red, flat line, code red, and we have a growing level of distrust," he added. He pointed to another decades-old technology — email — that we haven't completely figured out how to leverage for productivity yet either, which should caution executives as to the quick impact that AI could have. "Half of you right now are sitting here going, 'Man, how many emails are we going to have to deal with?' We've weaponized it to get more behind, and so we're walking a million miles an hour towards this AI nirvana, and we haven't even solved email productivity yet." What tech should do, Cadigan said, is "deliver a more beautiful world experience. Isn't that what we want technology for? More beauty, more joy, more time. And now we're seeing more anxiety, more depression, more suicide, more people freaking out." "The creation, the ability for us to create new technology, and that dissonance, I think, is a big, big problem," he added. - Colleen McKown 2 Hours Ago DailyPay's Nelson Chai: On-demand pay can help workers with financial strain watch now VIDEO 2:58 02:58 How companies can help employees stay financially afloat: DailyPay's Nelson Chai Americans are increasingly finding themselves strapped for cash amid the rising costs of groceries, gas and everyday expenses. That is leading more companies to begin to offer earned wage access as a benefit, which allows employees to access money they've already earned ahead of payday Nelson Chai, the CEO of on-demand pay platform DailyPay, told CNBC's Sharon Epperson about how the company's model works. "We have over 2,000 of the largest companies, including many that you've heard of, and we really go in and partner with them," he said. "If you had to wait 14 days to get paid, tomorrow you could go in and you could have access to your wages," he said. Employees are able to access their wages in a few different ways, he said. One option is to use the Daily Pay debit card, another is to do an ACH transfer, and another is to do a transfer to the bank of the employee's choice. "After you've taken out what you want to take out, then we send you the remainder of pay at the time of the normal paycheck," he said. "It's about meeting the workers where they are," he added. - Colleen McKown 2 Hours Ago Digital transformation is “two of the worst words ever used in the history of work” – former LinkedIn CHRO Steve Cadigan Steve Cadigan, Human Advantage Framework Creator and Author, speaks with CNBC's Leslie Picker at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 27, 2026. CNBC When Steve Cadigan was LinkedIn's chief human resources officer, he told CNBC's Leslie Picker at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit that a common trope at the networking platform was that whenever another company announced it was going through a digital transformation, that meant job cuts were on the horizon. "Let's look at all the people in the company that just announced a digital transformation and see who's looking for a new job," Cadigan told Picker. "When you tell employees we're going through a digital transformation, you're basically saying, 'Well, we care about the technology, not about you.'" While companies have heavily invested in AI tools, Cadigan said many have not "built the trust to get people to the point where they can say, 'Yeah, just go ahead and reinvent your job; we got your back.'" As more companies signal AI-driven job cuts, Cadigan said many employees see the first implementation of AI as "cutting people in the name of AI." Instead, Cadigan stressed that organizations need to promise to workers that they are investing in their growth and development, and that while they can't predict how AI will change their jobs or their future employment, these companies will "grow and develop you … we're going to make you a better human being and a better professional, and if things don't work out here, you're going to be a better person on the other side." "That's a bigger promise," he said. — Ian Thomas 3 Hours Ago The CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit is underway! Boeing also said it was targeting a production increase of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft in the second half of 2027. In this article BA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT VIDEO 6:41 06:41 Watch CNBC's full interview with Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production. CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month. Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected becuase of the wings production pace. Boeing stock was down about 10% in late afternoon trading. "I know everybody wants us to go faster but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday. Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday. "Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality." Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it. Third-quarter earnings The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit. For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program. Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025. The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion. Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG: Loss per share: 34 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 21 cents expected Revenue: $24.19 billion vs $23.84 billion expected. Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier. Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said. Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do." Certification wins The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet. And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line. headlines.article_text: Amazon memo shows AI coding guidelines, how it tackles tokenmaxxing Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon discouraged teams from relying solely on token usage or code generation as measurements of AI adoption, calling them "deeply flawed" metrics in an internal memo. Companies are grappling with rising AI costs and how to reliably measure whether the tools lead to a boost in productivity. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Amazon CEO Andy Jassy speaks at a company event in New York on Feb. 26, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools. The memo , which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI. "We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice." Under CEO Andy Jassy , Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs." As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment. Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing , in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks. Read more CNBC tech news A guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectus Nvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone Anthropic's IPO plans: 900% revenue retention, but $80 billion in first-half losses An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks. In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity. It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said. "We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote. Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity. The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said. "Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those." He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation." Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task. "If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo. Early third-quarter earnings show a 'resilient' U.S. consumer, with signs of strain
headlines.summary: Companies from Royal Caribbean to Coca-Cola and UPS say they are seeing steady consumer spending despite high inflation.
headlines.article_text: Q3 earnings show resilient U.S. consumer, signs of strain Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Companies from Royal Caribbean to Coca-Cola and UPS say they are seeing steady consumer spending despite high inflation. High fuel prices and interest rates raised concerns about slower consumer spending during the third quarter. Many businesses said they saw resilient spending in the third quarter, though some companies reported weaker sales. In this article KO WHR SHW UPS RCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A customer pushes a shopping cart with cases of Coca Cola outside a Walmart Supercenter retail store in North Bergen, New Jersey, U.S., Nov. 21, 2025. Mike Segar | Reuters One word keeps appearing in third-quarter earnings reports: "resilient." That's the early read on U.S. consumers from various companies that released their results this week. Many businesses say Americans are still spending despite inflationary pressures, though not every company has enjoyed the same success. The commentary comes amid fears that diesel fuel prices, which hit an all-time high of $6.52 per gallon in September, would drive up prices on consumer products . Economists also worried that more expensive regular gas, combined with high borrowing costs and continued tension between the U.S. and Iran, would spur a pullback in consumer spending. Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August. Sales in September were boosted by rising gas station spending. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales. While retail sales rose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August, the September came as gas station spending jumped. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales. "There's been a lot of noise in the market this year. There's a lot of geopolitical stuff," Royal Caribbean Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday. "But I look at our business [and our results], and I think that really talks to the resilience of the business, the resilience of the consumer." Royal Caribbean reported an increase in bookings during its third quarter, while Sherwin-Williams's CEO said the quarter was evidence of the company's strength. Here's how companies are reading the consumer in the most recent three-month period: Coca-Cola The food and beverage company beat analysts' expectations for third-quarter earnings and revenue despite what CEO Henrique Braun called an "uneven environment." Coca-Cola reported that North America unit case volume was flat, indicating demand was steady in the face of higher prices. The company's overall unit case volume was helped by higher demand outside of North America. "The underlying momentum remains quite strong," CFO John Murphy told CNBC. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that." The company increased its full-year forecast and now expects its comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from a prior forecast of growth between 9% and 10%. Royal Caribbean The cruise company beat Wall Street's expectations for earnings per share and narrowly missed on revenue. "Our third quarter results reflect continued strong consumer demand for our vacation experiences and the accelerated momentum across our industry leading brands," CEO Liberty said in the release . The company reported that the number of guests served in the third quarter increased 9% year over year to 2.7 million vacationers and said booking volumes for 2027 were already "up in the high teens," pacing ahead of historical levels and indicating high travel demand. "It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back as relates to the vacation experiences," Liberty told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" following the report. Royal Caribbean shares rose over 8% in Tuesday trading. watch now VIDEO 3:50 03:50 Royal Caribbean CEO Jason Liberty on Q3 earnings beat: We're seeing an uptick in bookings Squawk on the Street Sherwin-Williams Sherwin-Williams beat analysts' expectations for revenue but fell short of expected earnings per share. Sherwin-Williams CEO Heidi Petz said in the company's earnings release that the paint retailer's performance demonstrated "the resilience of our Company and the strength of our strategy in a challenging demand environment." "Despite muted underlying market volumes, we continued to win new customers, increase share-of-wallet and deliver sales growth across all three reportable segments," she said. Net sales increased 7.9% from the same period last year. The company attributed the gain to higher selling prices, but the benefits to profits were partially offset by increased costs of raw materials and supply-chain related expenses. And the company maintained full-year guidance, saying "customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027." UPS A worker drives a United Parcel Service (UPS) truck on Oct. 28, 2025 in Los Angeles, California. Mario Tama | Getty Images UPS beat Wall Street expectations for both earnings per share and revenue in the third quarter. Revenue in the U.S. rose 4.5% during the period to $14.86 billion. CEO Carol Tomé told investors on the company's earnings call that consumers remain "resilient" ahead of the holiday season, the company's busiest period. She said the company expects that average daily shipping volume will grow next quarter at a rate consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume will likely fall due to reducing deliveries with Amazon, she said. UPS has been in the midst of unwinding its partnership with Amazon at the same time it's executing a broad turnaround effort to operate more leanly. The company raised its full-year forecast for the second quarter in a row, projecting consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion. Shares rose more than 4% in Tuesday trading. Whirlpool Not every company is seeing the same spending trends, however. Appliance maker Whirlpool missed on both the top and bottom lines for its third quarter and cut its full-year revenue guidance. Net sales in North America fell more than 8% year over year during the period ending on Sept. 30. Even still, the company cited its own read on "resilience." "Through disciplined working capital management, we are protecting our year end free cash flow and our balance sheet resilience to navigate challenging market conditions," CFO Roxanne Warner said in the earnings release . Shares were down nearly 1% in Tuesday trading. — CNBC's Amelia Lucas and Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.
